name: Occam's razor
plain_explanation: Occam is famous for a principle -- though not, Russell notes, in the exact wording usually attributed to him -- that we should not multiply entities beyond what is strictly necessary to explain the facts. If a phenomenon can be fully explained without assuming some extra hypothetical entity, there is no ground for assuming that entity exists.
precise_definition: The methodological principle, associated with (though not verbatim from) William of Occam, that explanations should not posit more entities than are necessary; often rendered 'Entities are not to be multiplied without necessity,' closer to Occam's actual formulation 'It is vain to do with more what can be done with fewer.'
why_it_mattered: Russell states he has 'himself found this a most fruitful principle in logical analysis,' directly linking Occam's medieval logical practice to Russell's own twentieth-century philosophical method.
historical_origin: Attributed to William of Occam (ca. 1290-1349/50), though the exact phrase 'Entities are not to be multiplied without necessity' does not appear in his surviving works.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Explicitly endorsed and used by Russell in his own logical analysis; became a general methodological touchstone across later philosophy and science.
